title: The Potential of Biophilic Fractal Designs to Promote Health and Performance: A Review of Experiments and Applications
review_question: To review the evidence for how biophilic fractal designs promote human health and performance, and to discuss strategies for their application in the built environment.
inclusion_exclusion_criteria: Studies on human visual processing, physiological responses, aesthetic preferences, and performance in response to fractal patterns, particularly those found in nature and applied in architectural designs.

findings.consequent: Efficiency of human visual processing (eye saccade trajectories)
findings.quote: the eye follows long saccade trajectories when jumping between points of interest and smaller micro-saccades during dwell periods... traced out fractal patterns described by D = 1.4.
pupil dilation also varies in a fractal manner as the eye moves over the fractal images

findings.consequent: Brain activity (alpha and beta responses in qEEG)
findings.quote: the D = 1.3 fractals induced the largest changes in both alpha and beta responses
participants in behavioral studies exhibit increased sensitivity to mid-D fractals
could distinguish their D values more accurately
superior navigation through environments containing mid-D fractals
mid-D fractals induce large numbers of percepts... and that they activate the visual cortex's object perception and recognition regions
ninety-five per cent of people prefer fractal images over ones which have had their fractal content reduced
mid-D skylines being the most preferred
The stress saw-tooth was found to dampen when participants viewed mid-D fractals, indicating a stress-reduction of 60%

findings.antecedent: Fractal patterns (mid-D, projected on walls vs. displayed on monitors)
findings.quote: When fractal images are projected on the walls of a room rather than displayed on monitors, the preferred D shifts to higher values (D ~ 1.6-1.7)

findings.antecedent: Fractal patterns (mid-D, in artificial environments with Euclidean simplicity)
findings.quote: This introduction of Euclidean simplicity increases the tolerance for high fractal complexity

findings.antecedent: Fractal fluency (visual system as efficient fractal detector)
findings.quote: Fractal fluency pictures the visual system as an efficient fractal detector. This detection occurs well before conscious deliberations shape our aesthetic experiences.

findings.consequent: Structural rigidity, surface area to volume ratio, energy dissipation (noise, vibrations)
findings.quote: Eiffel employed the structural rigidity of a triangle at many different size scales... Fractals offer other practical advantages based on their large surface area to volume ratios, including large surfaces for solar panels and windows. The repeating structures can also dissipate the energy of impinging waves
Its D = 1.6 value was informed by the D = 1.6–1.7 target range suggested by the aesthetics experiments
our panels actively enhance the environmental aesthetics

findings.consequent: Visual comfort (obscuring unattractive views), shade provision, fractal shadow patterns, fractal breeze (dynamic fractals)
findings.quote: The fractal pattern can be used to obscure an unattractive view, it can provide shade, and it can also cast a fractal shadow pattern across a room. For open windows, the shade can also generate a fractal breeze.

findings.antecedent: Dynamic fractals (e.g., moving ripples, swaying branches, flickering flames, moving clouds)
findings.quote: the shades can generate dynamic fractals, which are expected to maintain the observer's attention to a higher degree than their static equivalents
is it possible for the visual system to perceive fractals without them being physically assembled? Discussions with artist Richard Downing led to him creating The Fractal Clock

The fractal patterns described here are increasingly referred to as biophilic fractals because they are likely responsible for biophilia's well-known effects, including the reductions in mental fatigue and stress

findings.antecedent: Lack of fractal aesthetics in unnatural (man-made) environments
findings.consequent: Visual system strain, negative responses (e.g., headaches)
findings.quote: the lack of fractal aesthetics in unnatural (man-made) environments puts a strain on the visual system, inducing negative responses such as headaches
Dynamic fractals also maintain attention.

findings.antecedent: Multisensory fractal experiences (visual, sonic, thermal, tactile – 'fractal atmosphere')
findings.quote: Imagine a future in which we immerse building occupants in synesthetic fractals—a 'fractal atmosphere' of visual, sonic, thermal, and tactile experiences—inducing an emergent experience that we have all evolved to expect and appreciate.

synthesis_conclusions: Human vision has adapted to efficiently process nature's fractal scenery, leading to enhanced visual performance, aesthetic preference, and physiological stress reduction.
Mid-range fractal complexity (D=1.3-1.5) is generally preferred and elicits optimal positive responses, including relaxation and arousal.
Integrating fractal patterns into the built environment through various applications (e.g., carpets, solar panels, window blinds, light patterns) can promote well-being and performance.
Dynamic and multisensory fractal designs hold significant potential for creating immersive, stress-reducing 'fractal atmospheres' in buildings.
The 'fractal fluency' model explains how the visual system is 'wired' to process fractals, leading to pre-conscious aesthetic experiences and health benefits.
evidence_gaps: Further fMRI studies are needed to understand the role of parahippocampal region and default mode network in fractal processing.
Research is needed to adapt bio-inspired fractal designs for artificial environments, rather than simply copying natural fractals.
The optimal rate of change for dynamic fractals needs to be determined.
Future behavioral experiments should use virtual environments to optimize preferred D values for specific room characteristics and functions (e.g., window, wall, floor, furniture obstruction).
Virtual environment findings need to be supplemented with on-site studies in real-life settings.
Future stress-reducing assessments should include cortisol tests in addition to skin conductance and EEG measurements.
Studies on on-site natural stimuli are more impactful than monitor-displayed images, suggesting a need for real-life settings research.
Investigation into whether aesthetic preferences for fractals evolve over time (adaptation) is crucial, especially for long-term exposure.
Exploration of the aesthetics of fractal sounds is an emerging research field.
Ongoing experiments are comparing visual and tactile impacts of physical 3D-printed fractal terrains.
Studies of on-site fractals are still in a preliminary phase, despite the Biophilia Hypothesis being nearly 50 years old.

moderators.variable: Viewing context (monitor vs. projected on walls)
moderators.effect: Shifts the preferred D value for fractal patterns (higher D preferred when projected on walls).
moderators.subgroup_effects: Preferred D ~ 1.4 for monitors, D ~ 1.6-1.7 for walls.

moderators.variable: Individual differences (genetic factors, personality traits, urban/rural living, aging)
moderators.effect: Influences fractal aesthetic preferences, leading to subgroups like 'sharpies' (high D preference) and 'smoothies' (low D preference).
moderators.subgroup_effects: Majority prefers mid-D, ~25% prefer high D, ~25% prefer low D.

limitations: The review acknowledges that 'one fractal will not fit all' due to individual differences in preference.
Studies of on-site fractals are still in a preliminary phase.
The initial aesthetic response to fractals is automatic, but conscious aesthetic experience also plays a role and is not fully explored.
The potential for adaptation to fractals over long exposure times (e.g., in an office) is a concern that needs further investigation.

paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: Fractal objects are prevalent in natural scenery. Their repetition of patterns at increasingly fine magnifications creates a rich complexity. Fractals displaying mid-range complexity are the most common and include trees, clouds, and mountains. The “fractal fluency” model states that human vision has adapted to process these mid-range fractals with ease. I will first discuss fractal fluency and demonstrate how it enhances the observer’s visual capabilities by focusing on experiments that have important practical consequences for improving the built environment. These enhanced capabilities generate an aesthetic experience and physiological stress reduction. I will discuss strategies for integrating fractals into building designs to induce positive impacts on the observer. Examples include fractal solar panels, fractal window shades, and fractal floor patterns. These applications of fractal fluency represent a fundamental and potentially impactful form of salutogenesis.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Natural environments, often characterized by fractal patterns, facilitate the restoration of directed attention.
Exposure to natural environments, including their fractal properties, can lead to physiological and psychological stress reduction.

The human visual system is adapted to efficiently process fractal patterns, particularly those with mid-range fractal dimensions (D=1.3-1.5), leading to aesthetic preference, reduced processing load, and positive physiological responses.

mechanism_chain.description: Fractal patterns, especially those with mid-range complexity (D=1.3-1.5), are processed efficiently by the visual system, leading to reduced cognitive load, increased aesthetic preference, and subsequent positive physiological and psychological outcomes.

Reduced cognitive load and increased perceptual fluency

steps.to_construct: Increased aesthetic preference and positive affect

steps.from_construct: Positive affect and reduced cognitive load
steps.to_construct: Physiological relaxation (e.g., lower heart rate, skin conductance) and improved cognitive performance (e.g., attention, memory)
